title: Dynamic arrays
learningGoals: make an array with a size known only at run time

youtube.title: C++ Dynamic Arrays: Size Chosen at Run Time | C++ Programming EP 47
youtube.description: In this episode you will make an array with a size known only at run time, free it correctly and explain why vector is safer, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Dynamic arrays · 0:57 Size from the user · 1:37 A pointer to n boxes · 2:07 Second program · 3:07 Recap · 3:39 Bug of the Day · 4:27 Challenge · 4:47 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "ANY SIZE" in tomato on lilac; Xecxec next to a box that grows to fit the order; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a box that grows to fit the order

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today the user chooses the size. A plain array cannot do this, but an array on the heap can.

scenes.onScreen: "Dynamic arrays": numbered lines (1. The size can come from the user; 2. You must free the array yourself; 3. A vector does the same job safely) and an analogy card: a tailor: he cuts the cloth only after you tell him your size
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A plain array needs a size that the compiler knows. An array on the heap can use a size that you read at run time. Use new with the size in square brackets. You must free it with delete square brackets. You must also remember its size yourself. This is why most programmers prefer a vector. Think of a tailor. He cuts the cloth only after you tell him your size.
points: The size can come from the user
You must free the array yourself
A vector does the same job safely

analogy.title: Dynamic arrays
analogy.body: A tailor: he cuts the cloth only after you tell him your size

scenes.onScreen: dyn.cpp: the user types the size, and the array fits
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 6] The user types the size. We use four. [HL 7] New makes an array with n items. The compiler did not need to know n. [HL 9] Each item gets the square of its position plus one. [HL 12] The output is one, four, nine, sixteen. [HL 15] We free the array at the end.

scenes.onScreen: a points to four boxes on the heap
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: N holds the size, four. A is a pointer on the stack. It points to the first of four boxes on the heap. Note that the pointer does not know the size. You must keep n yourself.

scenes.onScreen: safer.cpp: a vector does the same job in fewer lines
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 8] A vector with n items does the same job. [HL 10] We fill it in the same way. [HL 12] A range-based for works too. There is no new and no delete. The vector frees its own memory. It also knows its size.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as safer dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. Type four and press Enter. The program prints one, four, nine and sixteen.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. New with a size makes an array of any size at run time. Two. Free it with delete square brackets. Three. A pointer does not know the size of the array. Four. A vector is safer and shorter. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: New with a size makes an array of any size at run time.
Free it with delete square brackets.
A pointer does not know the size of the array.
A vector is safer and shorter.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Delete on a pointer to a local
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We call delete on n, which is a plain int. The compiler says the type int was given to delete, but a pointer is expected. Delete must get the pointer that new returned. Here that is a, and it needs square brackets.

scenes.onScreen: A tailor and a programmer have one thing in common. They both measure twice and cut once.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: A tailor and a programmer have one thing in common. They both measure twice and cut once.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: average of n numbers
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Ask for n. Make a vector of n numbers, read them, and print their average. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: memory leaks and RAII. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

dyn.cpp: In function 'int main()':
dyn.cpp:9:12: error: type 'int' argument given to 'delete', expected pointer
    9 |     delete n;
      |            ^
bug.why: Delete needs a pointer. The variable n is a plain int. Free the pointer that new returned, which is a.

pun: "A tailor and a programmer have one thing in common. They both measure twice and cut once."
challenge: Ask for n. Make a vector of n numbers, read them, and print their average.
challengeAnswer: Read n. Make vector of double with n items. Read each item with cin. Add them up, and divide by n.
